intro: Oahu's most remarkable trees cluster in four places. Foster Botanical Garden in downtown Honolulu holds five: a baobab, a Bodhi tree descended from the one in Bodh Gaya, a kapok older than the garden itself, a cannonball tree, and a soft-wooded quipo, all within a five minute walk behind one modest entrance fee. Moanalua Gardens keeps the Hitachi Tree, the rain tree famous from Japanese television. Thomas Square, Honolulu's oldest public park, keeps its banyans free to walk, and Ala Moana Beach Park keeps a tiered, geometric Black Olive free among its picnic lawns.
meta_description: Oahu's most remarkable trees: a baobab and a Bodhi tree in one Honolulu garden, the Hitachi Tree at Moanalua, free banyans and a Black Olive.
question_meta: Oahu's oldest confirmed tree is a kapok planted around 1851 in Foster Botanical Garden, roughly 175 years old. Full list of 8.
question_answer: Oahu's oldest documented tree is the Hillebrand Kapok in Foster Botanical Garden, planted around 1851 by the garden's founder, William Hillebrand, on what was then his own homestead. That makes it roughly 175 years old, older than the garden itself.
question_context: Foster Botanical Garden holds five of the eight trees on this page, and its own founding is younger than its oldest tree. William Hillebrand planted a kapok on his Honolulu homestead around 1851, decades before the property became a public botanical garden; it now stands about 27 metres tall with a trunk somewhere between four and seven metres around, depending on which of two disagreeing sources you read. Two more of the garden's trees carry documented arrival dates: a Bodhi tree grown from a cutting of the Bodh Gaya lineage, given to Mary Foster in 1913, and a baobab planted in the 1930s with a trunk already thirteen metres around. A cannonball tree and a quipo round out the five, both flagged for gaps rather than disputes. The other three trees on this page stand elsewhere, and all cost nothing to visit: the Indian banyans of Thomas Square, Honolulu's oldest public park, and the Geometry Tree of Ala Moana Beach Park, a Black Olive grown into flat, stacked tiers. The Hitachi Tree, a rain tree famous across Japan as a company emblem, is the one paid exception, eight kilometres away at Moanalua Gardens under a ticket of its own.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Oahu?
faq.a: The Hillebrand Kapok in Foster Botanical Garden, planted around 1851 by the garden's founder before the garden itself existed. It is roughly 175 years old.

faq.q: Where are Oahu's most remarkable trees?
faq.a: Five stand inside Foster Botanical Garden in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown, within a five minute walk of each other. The other three stand apart: the Hitachi Tree at Moanalua Gardens, and the free trees of Thomas Square and Ala Moana Beach Park.

faq.q: Is Foster Botanical Garden free to visit?
faq.a: No. Entry costs $1 to $5 for general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, with a $25 annual family pass. It is open 9am to 4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.

faq.q: Why do so many of Oahu's remarkable trees grow in one garden?
faq.a: Foster Botanical Garden began as the private collection of William Hillebrand and later Thomas and Mary Foster, who spent decades bringing in botanical curiosities from around the world before the city took the grounds over as a public garden. About twenty five of Oahu's roughly one hundred city-designated Exceptional Trees grow within its fourteen acres.

trees.name: The Foster Garden Baobab

location.address: 180 N. Vineyard Blvd, Honolulu, HI 96817 (Foster Botanical Garden)

verified_sources: https://data.honolulu.gov/resource/84fd-3fzf.json (City and County of Honolulu, Exceptional Trees register, register_id 1)
trees.access: Paid entry: $1-5 general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, $25 annual family pass. Open 9am-4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.
trees.transport: On N. Vineyard Blvd in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown; several TheBus routes run along Vineyard Blvd past the garden entrance.
trees.story:
Honolulu calls this one the Dead Rat Tree. The nickname is the seed pods: grey, furred, hanging on long stalks all around the crown, and once you have seen them you cannot unsee them. Under the pods is an African baobab, planted in Foster Botanical Garden in the 1930s and already carrying a trunk close to thirteen metres around. Ninety-odd years for that waistline is quick work, even for a species that grows a trunk largely to store water in it. The city's Exceptional Trees register gives its height as about twenty metres and rates its condition good.

Baobabs belong to dry African savanna, where they stand bare for months and flower at night for bats. This one has spent its whole life on fourteen acres of downtown Honolulu at the edge of Chinatown, on ground that was a private botanical collection long before the city took it over. It sat out a 1.26 million dollar renovation that closed the garden completely, and was still standing when the gates reopened in August 2023.

About twenty five of Oahu's hundred or so protected Exceptional Trees grow inside these same fourteen acres. That is the argument for the entrance fee: nowhere else on the island puts this many designated trees within a five minute walk of each other.

trees.name: The Foster Garden Bodhi Tree

location.address: 180 N. Vineyard Blvd, Honolulu, HI 96817 (Foster Botanical Garden)

verified_sources: https://data.honolulu.gov/resource/84fd-3fzf.json (City and County of Honolulu, Exceptional Trees register, register_id 420)
trees.access: Paid entry: $1-5 general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, $25 annual family pass. Open 9am-4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.
trees.transport: On N. Vineyard Blvd in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown; several TheBus routes run along Vineyard Blvd past the garden entrance.
trees.story:
The tree the Buddha is said to have sat under has descendants, and one of them grows in downtown Honolulu. This sacred fig was raised from a cutting of the Bodh Gaya lineage in India and arrived as a sapling in 1913, a gift to Mary Foster from Anagarika Dharmapala, the Sri Lankan reformer who spent his life campaigning to return that Indian temple to Buddhist hands. Foster planted it in her garden and went on to become a major patron of Buddhism in Hawaii, paying for the islands' first Buddhist temple.

The tree is about 113 years old now, roughly fifteen metres tall, with a trunk over seven metres around, and the city's Exceptional Trees register rates its condition excellent. Sacred figs are easy to identify once someone shows you the leaf: heart-shaped, drawn out into a long thin tail, hung so loosely on its stalk that the whole crown moves in air you cannot feel on your own skin. A tree that moves on a still day is the sort of thing people build religions around.

It is one of the few trees in this garden whose value has nothing to do with its size. There are bigger and far stranger specimens within a hundred metres of it. This is the one with a paper trail back to India and a woman who knew exactly what she had been given.

trees.name: The Hillebrand Kapok

location.address: 180 N. Vineyard Blvd, Honolulu, HI 96817 (Foster Botanical Garden)

verified_sources: https://data.honolulu.gov/resource/84fd-3fzf.json (City and County of Honolulu, Exceptional Trees register, register_id 116)
trees.access: Paid entry: $1-5 general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, $25 annual family pass. Open 9am-4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.
trees.transport: On N. Vineyard Blvd in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown; several TheBus routes run along Vineyard Blvd past the garden entrance.
trees.story:
The oldest tree in Foster Botanical Garden is older than the garden, because the man who planted it lived here first. William Hillebrand, the German physician and botanist who made this ground his homestead, put a kapok in at around 1851. That gives it roughly 175 years. It was already a mature tree when the Hawaiian Kingdom was overthrown in 1893, and a very large one when Pearl Harbor was bombed.

Its height is not in doubt. Honolulu Magazine and the city's Exceptional Trees register both give 88 and a half feet, about 27 metres, which is also how we know the two are describing the same trunk. The trunk itself they disagree on, and not by a little. The magazine reports 151 inches around, a shade under four metres. The register records 6.98 metres. The two have never been reconciled, so both stand here rather than one being quietly chosen. Some of the gap is probably method: a kapok throws out buttress roots like thin walls, and the answer changes depending on the height at which you measure.

Standing at the base, the buttresses are the point anyway. They rise past head height and divide the ground around the trunk into separate rooms, which is what a rainforest giant does when it has to hold itself up in shallow soil.

trees.name: The Foster Garden Cannonball Tree

location.address: 180 N. Vineyard Blvd, Honolulu, HI 96817 (Foster Botanical Garden)

verified_sources: https://data.honolulu.gov/resource/84fd-3fzf.json (City and County of Honolulu, Exceptional Trees register, register_id 118)
trees.access: Paid entry: $1-5 general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, $25 annual family pass. Open 9am-4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.
trees.transport: On N. Vineyard Blvd in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown; several TheBus routes run along Vineyard Blvd past the garden entrance.
trees.story:
The garden has put up a sign beside this tree warning visitors about falling cannonballs, and it is not a joke. Couroupita guianensis grows its fruit straight out of the trunk rather than from the branches, woody spheres somewhere between a grapefruit and a shot put, hanging on thick stalks that push out of the bark itself. Botanists call the habit cauliflory. Gravity calls it a hazard. A ripe one comes down from height and splits open with a smell that carries.

The flowers work the same way and are the reason to come: waxy, orange and pink, each one a shell-shaped hood over a dense spray of stamens, opening in ropes down the trunk at eye level while the crown sails on 29 metres above. It is a South American tree, from the Amazon and the Guianas, soft-wooded and fast, and the city's Exceptional Trees register rates this specimen's condition excellent. It is the most straightforwardly strange thing in a garden that is not short of competition.

One thing about it is missing: nobody has recorded when it went into the ground. If you know the planting date, or know someone at the garden who does, tell us and it goes on the page.

trees.name: The Foster Garden Quipo

location.address: 180 N. Vineyard Blvd, Honolulu, HI 96817 (Foster Botanical Garden)

verified_sources: https://data.honolulu.gov/resource/84fd-3fzf.json (City and County of Honolulu, Exceptional Trees register, register_id 114)
trees.access: Paid entry: $1-5 general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, $25 annual family pass. Open 9am-4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.
trees.transport: On N. Vineyard Blvd in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown; several TheBus routes run along Vineyard Blvd past the garden entrance.
trees.story:
This trunk is soft enough to cut with a knife. The quipo comes from the forests of Panama and Colombia, where it grows wood about as dense as balsa and gets felled for rafts and dugout canoes rather than for anything expected to hold weight. The tree wears that wood in a shape to match: smooth, greenish-grey, swollen low down and tapering upward, closer to a water tank than to anything with bark on it. Honolulu Botanical Gardens' own record puts the planting at 1930, which makes this one about 96 years old.

It has reached roughly 26 metres. That figure comes from the city's Exceptional Trees register alone and has not been checked against a second measurement, so treat it as the best number available rather than a settled one. Its seedpods are the other reason to look up: large, papery and winged, built to spin on the way down. The register rates the tree's condition excellent.

It stands near the centre of the garden, which is about right, because it is the specimen most visitors cannot name and cannot walk past either. Nothing else on these fourteen acres looks less like a tree, and that includes a baobab.

trees.name: The Hitachi Tree

location.address: Moanalua Gardens, 2850A Moanalua Road, Honolulu, HI 96819

trees.access: Paid entry, Moanalua Gardens admission (10 dollars), daily 08:30 to 16:00
trees.transport: About 8 km from Waikiki; TheBus routes along Moanalua Road stop by the gardens, and there is parking at the gate
trees.story:
This rain tree is on Japanese television most weeks, and almost nobody watching knows it is in Honolulu. Hitachi has used it as the company emblem since 1973, with a jingle that begins "this tree, what tree", and it is famous enough in Japan that visitors arrive at Moanalua Gardens asking for it by the company's name rather than the tree's.

What brought the advertising people here is obvious from the lawn. A rain tree grows outward rather than upward, and this one has spent about 130 years doing it: roughly 25 metres tall and a crown wide enough to shade some three thousand square feet of grass, held up on limbs that reach almost horizontally before turning. Stand under the middle and the canopy closes overhead like a roof.

The leaves do something worth timing your visit for. The leaflets fold shut in the late afternoon and before rain, which is where the name comes from, and the light through the canopy changes completely when they do. Hawaii knows the species as the monkeypod, and that is the name on the sign.

The gardens are privately owned and charge admission, which is unusual for a tree on this site and worth knowing before you drive out. The lawn around the trunk is open, so you can walk right up to it.

trees.name: The Banyans of Thomas Square

location.address: Thomas Square, 925 S Beretania St, Honolulu, HI 96814

trees.access: Free, public city park (Honolulu's oldest, dedicated 1850), open daylight into early evening, no admission.
trees.transport: Downtown Honolulu, at Beretania and Victoria Streets, across from the Honolulu Museum of Art; walkable from Waikiki or reachable by TheBus.
trees.story:
Honolulu's oldest public park did not always have shade. Thomas Square was set aside as parkland in 1850, but the banyans came decades later, when the Scottish merchant Archibald Scott Cleghorn took over as steward in 1882 and brought cuttings from Ainahau, his own Waikiki estate, to plant here. The overhauled park reopened to a brass-band crowd on 7 April 1887, and by the 1930s four banyans ringed the new central fountain, where they still stand.

They are Indian banyans, Ficus benghalensis, named in a University of Hawaii extension guide that singles out this exact grove as the reference specimen for the species in the islands, adding dryly that Disneyland's own banyan nearby is artificial. Cleghorn is better known today as the father of Princess Kaiulani and, later, Governor of Oahu; Ainahau, the estate these cuttings came from, held its own famous banyan, the one under which Robert Louis Stevenson used to read poetry to his young daughter.

Thomas Square has been public land since 1850, protected as a city park since 1925, and free to walk every day, no ticket and no gate, with King Street traffic on one side and the Honolulu Museum of Art across Beretania. Come toward evening and the fig-eating mynahs that roost here nightly make the banyans' size obvious from the noise alone.

trees.name: The Geometry Tree of Ala Moana Beach Park

location.address: Ala Moana Beach Park, 1201 Ala Moana Blvd, Honolulu, HI 96814

trees.access: Free, public city beach park, open 4am to 10pm daily, no admission.
trees.transport: Ala Moana Beach Park, between Waikiki and downtown Honolulu; TheBus stops along Ala Moana Blvd, and it borders Ala Moana Center, the shopping mall.
trees.verify_notes: Species, girth (320cm, checked consistent with the recorded 101.6cm diameter) and height (47ft/14.3m) come from the City and County of Honolulu's Exceptional Trees register (Act 105 of 1975, CC0), cross-checked against the department's own earlier printed survey of the same designation. Both are the same city program rather than fully independent sources, and no age is recorded anywhere, so this stays flagged. The register's coordinates are only grid-rounded to about 1.1km, so the pin marks the park itself (Wikipedia's own coordinate for the park matches the register's rounded point) rather than the tree's exact spot within it.
trees.story:
Ala Moana Beach Park has roughly forty banyans planted for its 1937 Banyan Garden, and one tree in the park belongs to none of them. Officially it is a Black Olive, Bucida buceras, but it earned its nickname, the Geometry Tree, from the way it grows: branches stack outward in flat, level tiers rather than the tangled shape most trees settle into. Some Black Olives are pruned hard to force that look; this one has done most of the work on its own.

The species is native to the Caribbean and Central America and arrived in Hawaii as a landscaping ornamental, prized for exactly this tiered habit. The City and County of Honolulu designated it an Exceptional Tree under the state's 1975 tree-protection law, recording a trunk just over three metres round and a crown reaching about fourteen metres, rated in excellent health at its last survey.

Ala Moana itself has been public land since the 1930s, built from reclaimed wetland into Honolulu's busiest beach park, free to enter every day between four in the morning and ten at night. No ticket, no gate, and the tree stands among the park's open lawns rather than off any marked path, worth hunting down once you know the odd, stacked shape to look for.
